newsitem.title: USA: Fed leaves interest rates unchanged.
newsitem.headline: Fed leaves interest rates unchanged.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
The Federal Reserve decided on Wednesday to hold interest rates steady, but many analysts believe it is only a matter of time before the inflation-wary central bank tightens credit.
The Fed's decision, disclosed after a two-day meeting, had been widely expected.
"Without any evidence of rising inflation, it's hard to justify raising rates," said David Wyss, of Massachusetts-based economic consultants DRI/McGraw Hill.
After advancing in early trading on hopes that the Fed would keep rates unchanged, stock and bond prices dropped in the afternoon to close lower.
The Dow Jones industrial average lost 86.58 points, mainly on selling of technology stocks, while bond prices fell on worries about next week's Treasury debt auctions.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan told state governors on Sunday that he saw no signs of significant price pressures in the economy, Iowa Gov. Terry Branstad said.
"He gave a positive report. We've had growth with low inflation," Branstad told reporters after the governors' closed-door meeting with the Fed chief.

The economy ended 1996 with a bang, growing at a 4.7 percent annualized rate in the final three months of the year. That was more than double the pace of the previous quarter and the fastest rate of growth in 2-1/2 years.
But inflation remained benign. The implicit price deflator that measures price changes rose at a mere 1.4 percent rate in the fourth quarter, the slowest pace since 1967.

In a sign that the economy may be about to slow from its torrid fourth-quarter pace, the government reported on Wednesday that factory orders ended 1996 on a weak note, falling 1.3 percent in December.
"They (Fed policy-makers) are gambling the economy will slow down and inflation will remain dormant," said Astrid Adolofson, of New York-based MCM MoneyWatch.
But many analysts are betting that will not happen without some action by the central bank.
With the job market taut and wages picking up, the Fed will eventually need to raise rates a notch if it wants to keep inflation in check, they said.
"One must be cautious in concluding that no action now precludes any move later in the quarter," said David Resler, of Wall Street broker Nomura Securities International.

Besides plotting interest rate strategy at their two-day meeting, Fed policy-makers also discussed their projections for economic growth, inflation and unemployment this year for presentation by Greenspan to Congress later this month.
Several Fed policy-makers have already said publicly that they expect moderate economic growth this year, in the 2 percent to 2-1/2 percent range.
On a fourth-quarter-on-fourth-quarter basis, the economy grew 3.4 percent last year.

But Chris Varvares, president of Macroeconomic Advisers of St. Louis, said there is a risk that inflation will pick up this year even if growth moderates because the economy is already running at such high level of capacity.

That eventually may prove enough to convince the Fed to take out some "monetary insurance" and raise rates a notch. But that will not happen until it can get a better reading of where the economy -- and inflation -- are headed, he said.
The Fed has held rates steady for over a year, since cutting them by a quarter percentage point on Jan. 31, 1996. Its next policy-making meeting is set for March 25.
The federal funds rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans stands at 5.25 percent; the discount rate that the Fed charges banks for money is 5 percent.
